This is my first blog post as a faculty member, and my first in almost four years. The last one went up in October 2022, a few months before I started my lab at Cornell. It was a revisit of a famous commentary by Jeff Leek, so it seems fitting to pick up exactly where I left off.

In 2013, Jeff Leek wrote a now-famous [blog post](https://simplystatistics.org/posts/2013-12-12-the-key-word-in-data-science-is-not-data-it-is-science) arguing that the key word in "data science" is science. In that 2022 post, I [revisited it](../keyword_data_science/index.qmd) with a simple 2x2 table: near-perfect or imperfect data on one side, near-perfect or imperfect science on the other. Good data with good science is a win-win, bad data with bad science is a lose-lose, and the two cells in between are where a data scientist earns their keep.

I wrote that a few weeks before large language models became everyday tools. Four years on, an AI assistant can clean a dataset, fit a dozen models, and write up the results in the time it takes to make a coffee. So it is fair to ask whether the 2x2 table still holds. I think it does, and I think its off-diagonal cells matter more than they did.

## What got cheaper

The mechanics of analysis: code, pipelines, standard models, the first draft of a report. In the "near-perfect data" column this is all gain. A simple model was already enough there, and now it arrives faster.

## What did not get cheaper

Knowing whether the answer is right. An AI system that is handed imperfect data still returns a fluent, well-formatted, confident result. "Garbage in, garbage out" has acquired a more dangerous cousin: garbage in, polished prose out. The lose-lose cell of the table now looks like a win on the surface, which makes the combination of imperfect data and imperfect science harder to spot than it was in 2013 or in 2022.

## Where the science lives now

In the same place Jeff Leek pointed to, with different day-to-day work:

- asking a question that the data can answer,
- understanding how the data were collected and what is missing from them,
- quantifying uncertainty, so that every prediction comes with an honest statement of how wrong it could be, and
- designing the check that would expose a wrong answer.

The last habit is the one I would teach first. When I ask an AI assistant for something consequential, the most valuable sentence in my request is the one that asks for proof: a comparison against a known answer, a held-out test, a validation that fluent writing cannot get around.

## The 2026 edition of the table

- Near-perfect data + AI: the win-win, only faster.
- Imperfect data + AI without scientific direction: the new lose-lose, and a well-disguised one.
- Imperfect data + AI directed by science: still the real test of a data scientist, and now within reach of many more people.

Thirteen years after Jeff Leek's post, the key word in data science is still science.
